subject: Biochemistry
vignette: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with new-onset generalized seizures and altered mental status. He has been vomiting and anorexic for 3 days. His family recently moved into a house built in 1920 that is undergoing renovation. Examination shows lethargy, pallor, and a lead line at the gingival margins. Blood lead concentration is 78 mcg/dL, and head imaging is unremarkable.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Observation with repeat blood lead measurement in 1 month
Parenteral dimercaprol combined with calcium disodium EDTA

explanation_correct: This child has lead encephalopathy, which is a medical emergency requiring prompt parenteral chelation with dimercaprol (British anti-Lewisite) plus calcium disodium EDTA, along with treatment of seizures and removal from the source of exposure. Oral chelators such as succimer are reserved for milder, asymptomatic elevations of blood lead. Delay in chelation in encephalopathy can result in permanent neurologic injury or death.

explanation_incorrect.A: Succimer is an oral chelator used for asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic children with lower blood lead concentrations; it is inadequate for lead encephalopathy because it is not given parenterally and acts more slowly.
explanation_incorrect.B: Iron supplementation treats iron deficiency anemia, not lead toxicity, and would not lower the blood lead concentration or treat the encephalopathy.
explanation_incorrect.C: Observation is inappropriate because encephalopathy and a blood lead concentration above 70 mcg/dL require urgent chelation rather than expectant management.
explanation_incorrect.D: Oral penicillamine is a second-line oral chelator and is not the initial treatment for severe lead poisoning with encephalopathy.

educationalObjective: Lead encephalopathy requires urgent parenteral chelation with dimercaprol plus EDTA, whereas oral succimer is reserved for less severe lead poisoning.
